    <rule name="dependency-levels">Assign tasks to the lowest level possible. Level 1 = no dependencies. Level N = depends on Level N-1 output. Never create circular dependencies.</rule>

    4. DATA-FLOW: Trace how data enters, transforms, persists, and exits the system

    6. TEST-DESIGN: Define requirements with WHEN/THEN scenarios and test specifications

    8. VERIFY: Cross-check every requirement has tasks, every task has test coverage, every story has criteria

    TESTABLE: Every requirement has concrete WHEN/THEN scenarios and test specifications
    SIZED: Each task is 10-30 minutes of focused work, not larger

# GitHub Issue #443: feat(c5c3-operator): replace the remaining static ExternalSecrets (keystone-admin, mariadb-root-password, k-orc-clouds-yaml) with operator-owned projection

**Description:**

`deploy/eso/externalsecrets/` still ships three statically applied ExternalSecrets — `keystone-admin.yaml`, `mariadb-root-password.yaml`, and `k-orc-clouds-yaml.yaml`, all listed in `deploy/eso/kustomization.yaml` and pulled into the production stack via `deploy/flux-system/infrastructure/kustomization.yaml:23` (`- ../../eso`). Each pins the default Quick Start identity (ControlPlane `controlplane` in namespace `openstack`), so bringing up a ControlPlane under any other name or namespace requires editing static manifests. This issue gives them the CC-0116 treatment that PR #442 (commit `407e8580`) established for `keystone-db`: operator-owned per-ControlPlane projection where a per-CR credential exists, production deletion plus a kind-only shim where only the standalone/dev flow needs the default identity, and outright consumer elimination where the manifest backs nothing on the critical path.

The work splits into one operator feature (Secret 1, the bulk of the change), one manifest relocation (Secret 2), and one consumer removal (Secret 3). The concrete boundaries:

**1. The structural template already exists; this issue adds its admin-password sibling.**
`operators/c5c3/internal/controller/reconcile_dbcredentials.go` is the merged CC-0116 pattern: a name-suffix constant (`dbCredentialSecretNameSuffix = "-db-credentials"`, line 29), a remote-key helper (`dbCredentialRemoteKeyFor`, lines 35-37), a name helper (`dbCredentialSecretName`, lines 42-44), a pure builder returning an `esov1.ExternalSecret` (the `external-secrets.io/v1` type, **not** `v1alpha1`) with `SecretStoreRef{Kind: "ClusterSecretStore", Name: openBaoClusterStoreName}` and `Target.CreationPolicy: esov1.CreatePolicyOwner` in `childNamespace(cp)` (`dbCredentialExternalSecret`, lines 52-67; `childNamespace(cp)` returns `cp.Namespace`, `reconcile_infrastructure.go:43-45`), and the sub-reconciler itself (`reconcileDBCredentials`, lines 83-150): brownfield early-exit, `controllerutil.CreateOrUpdate` with `SetControllerReference` inside the mutate closure (GC wired), then a `secrets.WaitForExternalSecret` gate (`internal/common/secrets/secrets.go:45-60` — it checks the **ExternalSecret object's** Ready condition, so a plain Secret can never satisfy it) requeuing with `dbCredentialsRequeueAfter` (10s, `requeue_intervals.go:23`).

This issue adds `operators/c5c3/internal/controller/reconcile_adminpassword.go`, a 1:1 mirror with these names (used consistently below):
- `adminPasswordSecretNameSuffix = "-admin-credentials"` (with the same `//nolint:gosec` G101 false-positive annotation the DB suffix carries).
- `adminPasswordSecretName(cp) = keystoneName(cp) + adminPasswordSecretNameSuffix` — default identity resolves to `controlplane-keystone-admin-credentials` (`keystoneName(cp) = cp.Name + "-keystone"`, `reconcile_keystone.go:29,41-43`).
- `adminPasswordRemoteKeyFor(cp) = fmt.Sprintf("bootstrap/%s/%s/admin", cp.Namespace, keystoneName(cp))` — default identity resolves to `bootstrap/openstack/controlplane-keystone/admin`, exactly the path today's `deploy/eso/externalsecrets/keystone-admin.yaml` reads. **Path-scoping nuance:** the admin path is keystone-name-scoped (`{ns}/{keystoneName(cp)}/admin`), unlike the cp-name-scoped DB path (`openstack/keystone/{ns}/{cp.Name}/db`). This matches both the seeder (`write-bootstrap-secrets.sh` seeds `kv-v2/bootstrap/${cp_ns}/${cp_name}-keystone/admin`) and the keystone-operator's Model B rotation PushSecret, whose RemoteKey is `bootstrap/%s/%s/admin` over `keystone.Namespace`/`keystone.Name` (`operators/keystone/internal/controller/reconcile_passwordrotation.go:604`) — and the projected Keystone child is named `keystoneName(cp)` in `cp.Namespace`, so read path and rotation write path land on the same key.
- `adminPasswordExternalSecret(cp)` — pure builder, one data entry `{SecretKey: "password", RemoteRef: {Key: adminPasswordRemoteKeyFor(cp), Property: "password"}}`, `RefreshInterval` 1h, owner reference left to the reconciler's mutate closure, mirroring `dbCredentialExternalSecret` line for line.
- `reconcileAdminPassword(ctx, cp)` — brownfield early-exit on `cp.Spec.Infrastructure.Database.ClusterRef == nil` (same discriminator as `reconcileDBCredentials`, per the issue) setting the condition `True` with reason `BrownfieldUserSuppliedCredential`; managed path `CreateOrUpdate` + `WaitForExternalSecret`, requeuing with a new `adminPasswordRequeueAfter = 10 * time.Second` in `requeue_intervals.go` (dedicated constant per the per-sub-reconciler naming convention documented at `requeue_intervals.go:18-23`), with condition reasons `ExternalSecretError`, `WaitingForAdminPasswordSecret` (not-ready), and `AdminPasswordReady` (ready) mirroring the DB reasons.

The per-CP-unique name is mandatory, not stylistic: `childNamespace(cp) == cp.Namespace`, so two ControlPlanes in one namespace would collide on a single `keystone-admin` Secret — the "Hardcoded sub-resource names prevent multi-instance support" failure CC-0116 fixed with `-db-credentials`.

**2. Condition and instrumentation wiring is established for six sub-reconcilers; this issue registers the seventh.**
- Add `conditionTypeAdminPasswordReady = "AdminPasswordReady"` to the constants block at `controlplane_controller.go:46-54`. The name must not collide with the existing `conditionTypeAdminCredentialReady = "AdminCredentialReady"` (line 51), which belongs to the K-ORC ApplicationCredential sub-reconciler — these are different credentials.
- Append it to `subConditionTypes` (`controlplane_controller.go:58-65`) so `setReadyCondition` (lines 168-186, via `conditions.AllTrue`) gates the aggregate `Ready` on it automatically.
- Add `"AdminPassword": conditionTypeAdminPasswordReady` to `subReconcilerConditionTypes` (`instrumentation.go:40-47`) so `instrumentSubReconciler` resolves the `condition_type` metric label instead of falling back to the `subReconcilerConditionTypeUnknown` (`"UNKNOWN"`) sentinel (`instrumentation.go:26,81-84`).
- Insert the chain call in `Reconcile` between the `DBCredentials` block (`controlplane_controller.go:111-115`) and the `Keystone` block (lines 117-121), using the same `instrumentSubReconciler(ctx, "AdminPassword", …)` + `!result.IsZero() || err != nil` early-return shape. Running before Keystone is load-bearing: the keystone-operator's `reconcileSecrets` gates `SecretsReady` on the admin Secret being backed by a **Ready ExternalSecret** (`operators/keystone/internal/controller/reconcile_secrets.go:119-133`, `WaitForExternalSecret(adminSecretKey)`, reason `WaitingForAdminCredentials`), so the ExternalSecret must exist before the Keystone child references it.
- The existing drift guard `TestSubReconcilerConditionTypesCoversAllNames` (`instrumentation_test.go:209`) asserts every map value is a member of `subConditionTypes` and must pass with the new entry. Note for the implementer: c5c3's `instrumentation.go` comments (lines 22, 36, 67) also cite a `TestSubReconcilerConditionTypesCoversAllCallSites` AST guard, but that test exists only in the keystone operator (`operators/keystone/internal/controller/instrumentation_test.go`) — the issue's "CC-0089 drift-guard / condition-coverage tests" maps to `TestSubReconcilerConditionTypesCoversAllNames` plus the `TestInstrumentSubReconciler_*` suite in this package; porting the AST guard is out of scope (Non-Goals).

**3. The defaulting webhook stays untouched; the projected child gets a managed-mode override.**
`controlplane_webhook.go` materializes `cp.Spec.KORC.AdminCredential.PasswordSecretRef = {DefaultAdminPasswordSecretName: "keystone-admin" (line 57), DefaultAdminPasswordSecretKey: "password" (line 64)}` at lines 159-164 — these defaults remain, exactly as `DefaultDatabaseSecretName = "keystone-db"` (line 46) survived CC-0116. What changes is the projection: `reconcile_keystone.go:131` currently passes the cp-level ref through verbatim (`keystone.Spec.Bootstrap.AdminPasswordSecretRef = cp.Spec.KORC.AdminCredential.PasswordSecretRef`). Replace it with `keystone.Spec.Bootstrap.AdminPasswordSecretRef = effectiveAdminPasswordSecretRef(cp)` (helper defined in boundary 4), mirroring the DB override at lines 123-124: managed mode points the child at the operator-owned Secret `{Name: adminPasswordSecretName(cp), Key: "password"}`; brownfield passes the user-supplied ref through untouched. `cp.Spec` is never mutated.

**4. This issue must repoint every cp-side reader of the admin password — a consumer the source issue's sketch does not call out, but its "converges to Ready" criterion requires (review pattern: "Trace every spec field to all its consumers").**
Two production code paths read the admin password by the cp-level ref today:
- `readAdminPassword` (`reconcile_korc.go:885-893`) resolves `cp.Spec.KORC.AdminCredential.PasswordSecretRef` and is called by `reconcileKORC` (line 356, to render the password-based clouds.yaml and the rotation hash) and by `computeAdminPasswordHash` (line 873, shared with the CredentialRotation reconciler).
- `controlPlaneSecretNameExtractor` (`controlplane_controller.go:201`) indexes ControlPlanes by `PasswordSecretRef.Name` so the Secret watch (`SetupWithManager`, lines 287-289) wakes the CP on admin-password rotation.

On a production cluster with the static manifest deleted, a Secret named `keystone-admin` never exists; `reconcileKORC` would loop forever on `KORCReady=False / WaitingForAdminPassword` (`reconcile_korc.go:357-368`) and the ControlPlane would never reach `Ready`. The kind shim masks this on the dev path only. Therefore add one helper in `reconcile_adminpassword.go`:

```go
// effectiveAdminPasswordSecretRef returns the SecretRef every cp-side consumer
// reads the admin password from: the operator-owned per-CP Secret in managed
// mode (Database.ClusterRef != nil), the user-supplied spec ref in brownfield.
func effectiveAdminPasswordSecretRef(cp *c5c3v1alpha1.ControlPlane) commonv1.SecretRefSpec
```

and use it in exactly three places: the `reconcile_keystone.go:131` override (boundary 3), `readAdminPassword` (replace the `ref :=` line at `reconcile_korc.go:886`; the `key == "" → "password"` fallback stays), and `controlPlaneSecretNameExtractor` (replace the `name :=` line at `controlplane_controller.go:201`, and update its doc comment plus the `ControlPlaneSecretNameIndexKey` doc comment at lines 32-39 to say the indexed value is the *effective* name — the index-key string constant itself stays unchanged, it is an opaque indexer label). `mark_eso_managed` already stamps the per-CP admin path in the seeder (CC-0109), so the rotation PushSecret keeps overwriting the same key the new ExternalSecret reads — the rotation loop stays closed with zero keystone-operator changes.

Ordering remains benign exactly as the issue states: `reconcileKORC` runs after Keystone (`controlplane_controller.go:123-127`) and already tolerates a not-yet-synced password via `WaitingForAdminPassword`; since `reconcileAdminPassword` gates on ExternalSecret readiness before Keystone even projects, the Secret exists by the time KORC reads it.

**5. Production removal and the kind-only shims (Secrets 1 and 2).**
- Delete `deploy/eso/externalsecrets/keystone-admin.yaml`, `deploy/eso/externalsecrets/mariadb-root-password.yaml`, and `deploy/eso/externalsecrets/k-orc-clouds-yaml.yaml`; reduce `deploy/eso/kustomization.yaml` to `resources: [clustersecretstore.yaml]` and update its header comment (the `externalsecrets/` directory disappears).
- Add `deploy/kind/infrastructure/keystone-admin-externalsecret.yaml`: ExternalSecret `keystone-admin` in `openstack`, store `openbao-cluster-store`, target `keystone-admin` / `CreationPolicy: Owner`, one data entry `password ← bootstrap/openstack/controlplane-keystone/admin` (property `password`) — byte-level shape of today's production manifest, with a header comment mirroring `deploy/kind/infrastructure/keystone-db-externalsecret.yaml`: standalone Keystone CRs (Quick Start, the `tests/e2e/keystone/*`, `tests/e2e-chaos/*`, and `tests/tempest/*` fixtures, plus `hack/run-tempest.sh`/`hack/ci-run-tempest.sh` which extract the admin password from this Secret) reference `keystone-admin` by name; ControlPlane deployments use the operator-projected per-CP ExternalSecret instead.
- Add `deploy/kind/infrastructure/mariadb-root-password-externalsecret.yaml`: ExternalSecret `mariadb-root-password` in `openstack`, one data entry `password ← infrastructure/mariadb` (property `root-password`), same content as today's production manifest, with a header explaining the Secret 2 rationale (next boundary).
- List both new files in `deploy/kind/infrastructure/kustomization.yaml` next to the existing `keystone-db-externalsecret.yaml` entry, extending that entry's explanatory comment block (review pattern: "Document intentional environment divergence in overlays").

**6. Secret 2 (`mariadb-root-password`) is relocation-only — option 1 of the source issue, decided here.**
This is not a per-ControlPlane service credential, so it gets no `reconcileDBCredentials`-style projection. The verified consumer set: the standalone Flux MariaDB baseline's `rootPasswordSecretKeyRef` (`deploy/flux-system/infrastructure/mariadb.yaml:43-45`); the `hack/deploy-infra.sh` force-sync loop (line 1216) and Step 8 wait (lines 1223-1224); and the `tests/e2e/infrastructure/infra-stack-health/chainsaw-test.yaml` assertion (the ExternalSecret Ready block around lines 190-198). The operator-managed path is already dead weight: `ensureMariaDB` (`reconcile_infrastructure.go:166-173`) sets no `rootPasswordSecretKeyRef` at all — mariadb-operator generates its own root Secret per managed cluster. Relocating the manifest to the kind overlay keeps every consumer green on kind. One consequence must be documented, not coded around: a non-kind deployment of the Flux MariaDB baseline now has to provide the `mariadb-root-password` Secret itself (own ExternalSecret or plain Secret) — add this prerequisite note to `docs/reference/infrastructure/infrastructure-manifests.md`, which already discusses the root-password race at lines 832-835 and the source Secret at line 593. The Step 8 force-sync loop (`for es in keystone-admin keystone-db mariadb-root-password`, line 1216) and the `wait_for_externalsecrets "openstack" … keystone-admin keystone-db mariadb-root-password` call (lines 1223-1224) keep working verbatim — the kind shims materialize the same three ExternalSecrets in `openstack`. **Motivation:**

The three manifests under `deploy/eso/externalsecrets/` are the last static, single-identity credential shims in the production deploy stack. <baseline-guidelines>
<purpose>Foundational behavioral baseline applied to every generated prompt.
Reduces common LLM coding mistakes by biasing toward caution, simplicity,
surgical changes, and verifiable goals. For trivial tasks, use judgment —
these guidelines bias toward correctness over speed.</purpose>

<principle name="think-before-coding" order="1">
  <rule>Before implementing: state assumptions explicitly.</rule>
  <rule>If multiple valid interpretations exist, name them — never pick silently.</rule>
  <rule>If a simpler approach exists, surface it. Push back when warranted.</rule>
  <rule>Make tradeoffs visible — do not hide confusion.</rule>

  <ambiguity-resolution priority="critical">
    <rule phase="planning,elaboration,analysis,research,chat,review">
      In planning, analysis, research, review, or chat phases: surface ambiguity
      as Open Questions. Ask the user when clarification is genuinely needed.
    </rule>
    <rule phase="implementation,improvement,simplification,fix,chore">
      During implementation, improvement, simplification, fix, or chore phases:
      NEVER ask the user. Instead: (1) conduct deep research — search the
      codebase, read docs, analyze similar patterns; (2) make the best possible
      decision autonomously; (3) leave a clearly visible `# DECISION:` comment
      at the decision point so reviewers can find and evaluate it.
    </rule>
    <decision-comment-format>
      # DECISION: [What was unclear] — Chose [X] because [reasoning]. Reviewer: please verify.
    </decision-comment-format>
    <rationale>Keeps implementation velocity high while making every judgement
    call transparent and reversible.</rationale>
  </ambiguity-resolution>
</principle>

<principle name="simplicity-first" order="2">
  <rule>Write the MINIMUM code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.</rule>
  <rule>No features beyond what was asked.</rule>
  <rule>No abstractions for single-use code — require 2+ concrete callers first.</rule>
  <rule>No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.</rule>
  <rule>No error handling for impossible scenarios — validate at system boundaries only.</rule>
  <rule>If you wrote 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.</rule>
  <self-check>"Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.</self-check>
</principle>

<principle name="surgical-changes" order="3">
  <rule>Touch only what you must. Match existing style even if you would do it differently.</rule>
  <rule>Do NOT "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting unrelated to the task.</rule>
  <rule>Do NOT refactor things that aren't broken.</rule>
  <rule>If you notice unrelated dead code, MENTION it — do not silently delete it.</rule>
  <rule>Only remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.</rule>
  <rule>Do NOT remove pre-existing dead code unless explicitly asked.</rule>
  <test>Every changed line must trace directly to the user's request. If a line
  cannot be justified by the task spec, it does not belong in the diff.</test>
</principle>

<principle name="goal-driven-execution" order="4">
  <rule>Transform vague tasks into verifiable goals before starting.</rule>
  <transformations>
    <example from="Add validation">Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass.</example>
    <example from="Fix the bug">Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass.</example>
    <example from="Refactor X">Ensure tests pass before AND after.</example>
  </transformations>
  <rule>For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan with verification per step:
    1. [Step] → verify: [check]
    2. [Step] → verify: [check]
    3. [Step] → verify: [check]
  </rule>
  <rule>Loop until every verification check passes. Strong success criteria let
  you self-validate without constant clarification.</rule>
</principle>

<application>
  <rule>These principles apply to EVERY generated prompt as baseline behavior.</rule>
  <rule>For trivial tasks (one-line fixes, typos), apply judgment — strict adherence is unnecessary overhead.</rule>
  <rule>When these principles conflict with task-specific guidelines, task-specific guidelines win.</rule>
</application>
</baseline-guidelines>


<critical-rules priority="blocking">
  <!-- Reasoning depth is controlled by the Claude CLI effort flag (see [claude] effort in settings.toml). Do not issue conflicting thinking-budget instructions in-prompt. -->
  <!-- DECISION: Placed in core_rules (id=0) rather than baseline because CORE_RULES is the
       constant injected into both the review and implementation builds, so a single edit reaches
       both. superpowers reports this one clause is what finally made their discipline rules hold.
       Reviewer: please verify it should be global rather than per-phase. -->
  <rule id="0" name="LETTER_EQUALS_SPIRIT" priority="blocking">
    <requirement>Violating the letter of these rules is violating their spirit. "I'm just being pragmatic", "only this once", and "the rule clearly didn't mean this case" are violations, not exceptions.</requirement>
    <violation>Rule-lawyering to justify a shortcut is treated as breaking the rule outright</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="1" name="LANGUAGE">
    <requirement>All output in English (code, comments, commits, docs)</requirement>
    <violation>Non-English output rejected</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="2" name="NO_OUTPUT_COMMENTARY">
    <requirement>Keep the final output direct: no prose preambles, no meta-commentary, no restating of intent before acting. Internal reasoning (extended thinking blocks) is expected and must not be suppressed — this rule governs the visible output only.</requirement>
    <examples>
      <bad>Final output begins with "Let me first understand...", "This is a great example...", "I'll now..."</bad>
      <good>Final output states results and necessary status directly; reasoning lives in thinking blocks</good>
    </examples>
    <violation>Verbose preambles in the final output waste tokens; thinking blocks are fine</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="3" name="NO_COMMITS">
    <requirement>Never run git commit - planwerk handles git operations</requirement>
    <violation>Manual commits break tracking, will be reverted</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="4" name="MINIMAL_CHANGES">
    <requirement>Only modify files directly related to current task</requirement>
    <violation>Unrelated changes reverted during review</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="5" name="FOLLOW_PATTERNS">
    <requirement>Search codebase for existing patterns before creating new</requirement>
    <violation>Redundant implementations rejected</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="6" name="NO_SCOPE_CREEP">
    <requirement>Implement only what is explicitly requested</requirement>
    <violation>Extra features removed, effort wasted</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="7" name="TYPE_SAFE">
    <requirement>All code must pass mypy (Python), tsc (TypeScript), or go vet (Go) strict checks</requirement>
    <violation>Type errors block merge - no type: ignore without justification</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="8" name="LINT_CLEAN">
    <requirement>All code must pass ruff (Python), eslint (TypeScript), or golangci-lint (Go) without errors</requirement>
    <violation>Lint errors block merge - run ruff check/eslint/golangci-lint before completion</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="9" name="TEST_COVERAGE">
    <requirement>New/modified code must have accompanying tests - no untested code</requirement>
    <violation>Untested code rejected in review - write tests FIRST (TDD)</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="10" name="NO_BASH_TASKS">
    <requirement>Use native TaskCreate/TaskList/TaskUpdate for task management — never Bash scripts or filesystem workarounds</requirement>
    <violation>Bash-based task creation is fragile and breaks tracking</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="11" name="FEATURE_ID_REQUIRED">
    <requirement>When referencing requirements, tests, tasks, or user stories in docs, docstrings, comments, or commit messages — ALWAYS include the Feature ID</requirement>
    <examples>
      <bad>"Fixes the login bug", "See related task", "As per requirement"</bad>
      <good>"Fixes login bug (F-0042)", "See task F-0042", "As per requirement F-0042"</good>
    </examples>
    <violation>References without Feature ID are untraceable and rejected in review</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="12" name="NO_SUBMODULE_MODIFICATIONS">
    <requirement>In a worktree, NEVER modify files inside a git submodule. Submodule content is strictly READ-ONLY from the worktree's perspective — it serves EXCLUSIVELY as a source of information (read, grep, reference). Never Edit, Write, patch, format, lint-fix, or otherwise change submodule files. Before editing any file, verify its path is NOT inside a submodule (check `.gitmodules` or `git submodule status`). If a task appears to require a submodule change, STOP and report it instead of proceeding.</requirement>
    <examples>
      <bad>Editing a file whose path falls under a submodule directory listed in `.gitmodules`</bad>
      <bad>Running a formatter/linter that writes to submodule files</bad>
      <good>Reading/grepping submodule code for context, then applying all changes to the parent repository only</good>
    </examples>
    <violation>Submodule writes from a worktree cross independent git contexts, produce untracked/inconsistent state across repos, and will be reverted</violation>
  </rule>
</critical-rules>


<planning-process>
1. SCAN for available project documentation (README.md, PLAN.md, docs/, other doc files) — use whatever exists
2. EXTRACT content relevant to this specific feature from all available doc sources
3. SEARCH codebase for similar features/patterns and existing utilities
4. IDENTIFY existing test conventions
5. CREATE the planning artifacts below
6. CROSS-REFERENCE generated tasks against doc-described functionality — no gaps allowed
</planning-process>

<fullstack-checklist required="before-finalizing">
□ Backend API endpoint(s) with tests
□ Frontend API client hook(s)
□ Frontend UI component(s) with user interaction
□ If admin feature: Admin/management UI coverage
□ All layers connected and working together
</fullstack-checklist>
<planning-guidelines>
<thinking required="before-planning">
  <step order="0" name="CHALLENGE">Before any technical analysis, challenge the problem definition itself:
    (a) Is the scope appropriate? Can it be reduced without losing core value? (Scope Reduction mode)
    (b) Is the scope as stated sufficient to solve the actual problem? (Standard mode)
    (c) Does the scope need expansion to avoid a half-solution? (Expansion mode)
    Pick the right mode and document the rationale. This prevents building the wrong thing well.

    <scope-decision-framework>
      <principle name="completeness-is-cheap">When AI compresses implementation effort 10-100x,
      prefer the complete solution over incremental delivery. The cost of re-planning and re-contextualizing
      exceeds the cost of AI-generating the complete feature in one pass.</principle>
      <when-to-expand>
        <signal>Feature has natural sub-features that users will immediately request after delivery</signal>
        <signal>Error-handling paths are obvious and the complete set is enumerable</signal>
        <signal>CRUD has only C and R — add U and D upfront to avoid a second planning cycle</signal>
        <signal>Validation rules are partially specified — complete the full set rather than leaving gaps</signal>
      </when-to-expand>
      <when-to-reduce>
        <signal>Feature touches unfamiliar external systems with unknown behavior — minimize assumptions</signal>
        <signal>Requirements are genuinely ambiguous — implement minimum, validate with user</signal>
        <signal>Task sizing would exceed a single context window even after splitting</signal>
        <signal>Feature depends on decisions not yet made (e.g., pending design review)</signal>
      </when-to-reduce>
      <clarification>This does NOT contradict MINIMAL_CHANGES or NO_SCOPE_CREEP from core_rules.xml —
      those apply during IMPLEMENTATION (do exactly what was planned). This framework applies during
      PLANNING (decide how complete the plan should be). Plan thoroughly, implement precisely.</clarification>
    </scope-decision-framework>
  </step>
  <step order="1" name="SCOPE">What exactly is being requested? What is explicitly OUT of scope?</step>
  <step order="2" name="LAYERS">Which layers are affected (backend, frontend, hooks, tests)?</step>
  <step order="3" name="DEEP_RESEARCH">Conduct systematic multi-angle codebase research (see deep-research skill):
    (a) Broad Exploration: Survey the affected area — search by feature/entity name, read project docs (README.md, PLAN.md, docs/, architecture/ as read-only reference)
    (b) Deep Dive: For each dimension (model, API, service, tests, config), READ the actual implementations. Follow imports and references.
    (c) Diversity: Examine patterns, data flow, error handling, tests, dependencies, and configuration for analogous features — ensure no blind spots
    (d) Synthesis Check: Verify you can answer: What patterns to follow? Which files affected? Integration points? How similar things are tested?
    Do NOT proceed to planning until research is complete.</step>
  <step order="4" name="EXISTING">What similar features exist that I should follow? (should be answered by deep research)</step>
  <step order="4.5" name="PATTERN_CAPTURE" priority="critical">
    After deep research, check discovered patterns against mandatory patterns:
    (a) Read pattern files loaded in <mandatory-patterns> above
    (b) For each recurring pattern found 2+ times in codebase that is NOT yet captured:
        CREATE a file in the patterns directory (kebab-case.md)
        Format: # Pattern: ..., **Component**, **Category**, **Applies-When**,
        ## Structure, ## Example, ## Anti-Pattern (under 1500 chars body)
    (c) Only for RECURRING patterns (2+ occurrences) — not one-off implementations
    (d) Reference created patterns in implementation_notes
  </step>
  <step order="5" name="DEPENDENCIES">What needs to be done first? What can be parallelized?</step>
  <step order="6" name="RISKS">What could go wrong? What needs extra testing?</step>
  <step order="7" name="EDGE_CASES">What edge cases, error states, and boundary conditions exist?
    Shadow Path Tracing: For every data flow, systematically map what happens at each step for:
    nil/None, empty collections, error responses, timeouts, partial failures, malformed input.
    Build a failure mode registry — each failure mode gets an explicit handling strategy.</step>
  <step order="8" name="DATA_FLOW">How does data flow through the system for this feature?</step>
</thinking>

<comprehensiveness priority="critical">
  The specification MUST be MORE detailed than the elaboration. Every aspect broken into concrete, actionable items.
  Include error handling, edge cases, validation, security. Each component maps to specific stories, requirements, tasks.
  Self-contained: implementer needs NOTHING beyond this document.
</comprehensiveness>

<completeness-requirement priority="critical">
  Every function, endpoint, component, and behavior described in the feature description,
  docs/, architecture/ (read-only), README.md, or PLAN.md MUST have corresponding tasks. No stubs, no placeholders,
  no "TODO" implementations. Each task must result in FULLY WORKING, TESTED code.
  If a feature description mentions a capability, there MUST be a task that implements it completely.
  CROSS-REFERENCE CHECK: After drafting tasks, re-read the feature-relevant sections from ALL
  available documentation sources. For each doc-described capability, verify a task exists.
  Add missing tasks if any gap is found.
</completeness-requirement>

<task-sizing priority="critical">
  <rule>Each task MUST be completable in ONE agent iteration (one context window).
  If a task requires understanding more code than fits in context, the agent will stub the rest.</rule>

  <right-sized>
    <example>Add a database column and migration</example>
    <example>Add one API endpoint with validation and tests</example>
    <example>Add one UI component to an existing page</example>
    <example>Add a filter dropdown to a list view</example>
    <example>Refactor one function/class with its tests</example>
  </right-sized>

  <too-big reason="Agent runs out of context, stubs remaining work">
    <example bad="Build the entire dashboard">Split: schema, queries, UI components, filters — each a separate task</example>
    <example bad="Add authentication">Split: schema/migration, middleware, login UI, session handling</example>
    <example bad="Refactor the API layer">Split: one task per endpoint or per pattern change</example>
    <example bad="Add notification system">Split: DB table, notification service, bell icon, dropdown panel, mark-as-read, preferences page</example>
  </too-big>

  <splitting-rule>If you cannot describe the change in 2-3 sentences, it is too big. Split it.</splitting-rule>
  <splitting-rule>Each split task must be independently testable and verifiable.</splitting-rule>
  <splitting-rule>After splitting: verify no task depends on a later task (dependency order).</splitting-rule>
</task-sizing>

<verifiable-criteria priority="critical">
  <rule>Every acceptance criterion MUST be something the agent can CHECK — not something vague.</rule>

  <good label="Verifiable">
    <example>Add `status` column to tasks table with default 'pending'</example>
    <example>GET /api/features returns 200 with list of Feature objects</example>
    <example>Filter dropdown has options: All, Active, Completed</example>
    <example>Clicking delete shows confirmation dialog before removing</example>
    <example>Invalid email input returns 422 with field-level error message</example>
  </good>

  <bad label="Vague — agent cannot verify these">
    <example>Works correctly</example>
    <example>User can do X easily</example>
    <example>Good UX</example>
    <example>Handles edge cases</example>
    <example>Properly integrated</example>
  </bad>

    <criterion context="every-task">Typecheck passes (mypy/tsc/go vet)</criterion>
    <criterion context="every-task">Lint passes (ruff/eslint/golangci-lint)</criterion>
    <criterion context="tasks-with-logic">All tests pass</criterion>
    <criterion context="tasks-with-ui">Visual verification in browser</criterion>

<user-stories min="5" note="minimum floor, generate MORE if needed for full coverage">
  <rule>Cover ALL layers: backend API, frontend UI, hooks, error handling</rule>
  <rule>Include operator/admin perspectives if applicable</rule>
  <rule>Each story has min 4 testable acceptance criteria - be specific, not generic</rule>
  <rule priority="critical">Concrete, not abstract: every acceptance criterion states an OBSERVABLE outcome with exact values, inputs, and named entities. Ban "works correctly", "as expected", "handles many cases" — give the exact case and the expected result.</rule>
  <rule>Include negative stories (what should NOT happen, error cases)</rule>
  <rule>Cover the complete user journey, not just the happy path</rule>
  <rule>Stories must address: creation, reading, updating, deletion, validation, error states</rule>
  <rule>Include documentation stories: Reference docs for APIs/components, How-to guides for user-facing features</rule>
  <rule priority="critical">Generate exactly as many stories as the feature REQUIRES. The minimum is guidance to avoid under-specification, not a target. If the feature only needs 3 stories, generate 3. If it needs 10, generate 10. Never pad with redundant or near-duplicate stories just to reach the minimum, and never omit a needed story to stay low.</rule>
</user-stories>

<documentation-requirements>
  <quadrants framework="Diataxis" source="https://diataxis.fr/">
    <quadrant name="reference" priority="SHALL">Information-oriented: APIs, schemas, config. Required for ALL new APIs, components, data models.</quadrant>
    <quadrant name="how-to" priority="SHALL" scope="user-facing">Task-oriented: step-by-step guides. Required for features with user interaction (UI, CLI, external API). Internal-only features exempt.</quadrant>
    <quadrant name="tutorials" priority="MAY">Learning-oriented: guided exercises. For complex workflows spanning 3+ components.</quadrant>
    <quadrant name="explanation" priority="MAY">Understanding-oriented: context, rationale. For new patterns or non-obvious architectural choices.</quadrant>
  </quadrants>

  <content-rules>
    Reference: endpoint path+method, request/response schemas with types, error codes | Component: props table, usage example | Data model: field table with constraints, validation rules
    How-to: Prerequisites → numbered Steps → Verification → See Also (Reference docs)
    Tutorials: learning objectives, hands-on exercises, gradual complexity, working examples
    Explanation: problem context, alternatives considered, decision rationale, focus on WHY
  </content-rules>

  <file-paths>
    <structure>{docs_dir}/{quadrant}/{component_type}/{artifact_name}.md</structure>
    <quadrants>reference, how-to, tutorials, explanation</quadrants>
    <component-types>backend, frontend, models</component-types>
    <note>docs_dir configured in build_focus_areas() in planwerk/config.py</note>
  </file-paths>

  <task-granularity>
    Single artifact (1 endpoint/component): one Reference task, 10-15 min |
    Grouped artifacts (CRUD for one resource): one Reference task, 20-30 min |
    Complex features: separate How-to tasks from Reference tasks, How-to references Reference docs
  </task-granularity>
</documentation-requirements>

<requirements min="8" note="minimum floor, generate MORE if needed for full coverage">
  <rule>Use RFC 2119 priorities: SHALL (mandatory), SHOULD, MAY</rule>
  <rule>Each requirement has at least 3 WHEN/THEN scenarios (happy path, error case, edge case)</rule>
  <rule>SHALL requirements are blocking for completion</rule>
  <rule>Include requirements for: validation, error handling, performance, security, accessibility</rule>
  <rule>Each requirement description must be precise and unambiguous - no vague language</rule>
  <rule>Concrete, not abstract: describe the observable behavior with exact values, limits, and status codes — not intentions. Replace "handles errors gracefully" with the exact error, status code, and message.</rule>
  <rule>Requirements must cover ALL data flows: input validation, processing, output formatting, error propagation</rule>
  <rule>Include non-functional requirements: response times, data limits, concurrent access</rule>
  <rule priority="critical">Generate exactly as many requirements as the feature REQUIRES. The minimum is guidance to avoid under-specification, not a target. If the feature only needs 5 requirements, generate 5. If it needs 20, generate 20. Every distinct behavior, validation rule, or constraint deserves its own requirement — but do NOT create redundant or artificial requirements just to reach the minimum count.</rule>
</requirements>

<test-specifications note="at least 2 per requirement, more if the requirement has more scenarios">
  <rule>At least 2 test specifications per requirement — more if the requirement has more WHEN/THEN scenarios</rule>
  <rule>Cover positive tests, negative tests, and boundary conditions</rule>
  <rule>Specify exact file paths following project conventions</rule>
  <rule>Each test must have a clear expected outcome description</rule>
  <rule>Include integration tests that verify cross-component behavior</rule>
  <rule>Every WHEN/THEN scenario in a requirement SHOULD have a corresponding test specification</rule>
  <rule priority="critical">Edge cases MUST have dedicated test specifications — they must NEVER be dropped or silently absorbed into happy-path tests. Boundary conditions, error states, empty inputs, invalid data, concurrent access, and overflow scenarios each deserve explicit test coverage.</rule>

  <test-tier-coverage priority="critical">
    <rule>During DEEP_RESEARCH, scan the project for existing test tiers: unit tests (tests/unit/), integration tests (tests/integration/), E2E tests (tests/e2e/ or tests/end_to_end/). Record which tiers exist.</rule>
    <rule>Test specifications MUST cover ALL tiers that already exist in the project:
      - Unit tests: isolated function/class behavior with mocked dependencies
      - Integration tests: cross-component interaction, real database/service calls
      - E2E tests: full user workflow from entry point to final result
